summary:
Team Nebulla presents Nebulla Space Relics, an interactive, animated educational web platform built for the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge. Since the dawn of space exploration, NASA has left rovers, landers, and scientific instruments scattered across the Moon, Mars, and deep space. While these artifacts are retired, their stories and engineering legacies remain vital. 

Our solution transforms static space history into an engaging, first-person storytelling experience tailored for students and space enthusiasts aged 10–15. Built using lightweight HTML5, CSS3 animations, and vanilla JavaScript and hosted live via GitHub Pages, the platform features interactive solar system modules, hardware diaries, engineering specifications, and a junior space historian quiz. By bridging historical hardware data with immersive web design, Nebulla Space Relics inspires the next generation of space explorers to understand and appreciate humanity's enduring footprint across the cosmos.
details:
Project Overview

Since the 1960s, NASA has deployed extraordinary spacecraft, rovers, and scientific instruments across the solar system—from the surface of the Moon and Mars to the far reaches of deep space. While many of these missions have completed their primary objectives or remain traveling far beyond Earth, the hardware they left behind represents humanity's greatest milestones in exploration and engineering.

Created by Team Nebulla, this interactive web application transforms the history of NASA's discarded and retired equipment into an engaging, story-driven journey tailored specifically for school-age space enthusiasts. Instead of static textbook facts, users explore a dynamic, animated solar system interface where each piece of hardware tells its own first-person story—connecting how it was built, what happened to it, and the groundbreaking science it made possible.

Key Features

  • Interactive Solar System Explorer: Users navigate across distinct cosmic zones—the Moon (Apollo lunar hardware and retroreflectors), Mars (retired rovers and landers), and Deep Space (long-distance probes still venturing outward)—through smooth scroll animations and interactive visual cards.
  • First-Person Hardware Diaries: Every spacecraft and instrument features an accessible, narrative-driven "My Story" perspective alongside mission timelines, current operational status (dormant vs. active), key engineering highlights, and the scientific discoveries unlocked by the mission
  • Interactive Space Historian Quiz: An integrated self-check challenge that reinforces core concepts and rewards young learners upon completion.

How It Was Built : Built as a fast, lightweight, single-page web application using HTML5, CSS3 keyframe animations, inline SVG illustrations, and vanilla JavaScript—requiring zero external dependencies so students, educators, and judges can access it seamlessly on any device.
